rv.q: It's a huge, troubling subject, given a witty, imaginative treatment. But the show feels rather packed and restless: so fearful of being boring that it whistles through material too fast for you to absorb it.
It's an interesting project that wears its politics on its sleeve, with moments that sparkle. But it left me with a presiding feeling that I'd been trapped in a revision session.
But the ingredients are not melded together: anecdote and didacticism fight each other.
But the finished piece is bitty, flimsy and, in places, hard to follow.

This is an evening of muddled, sandblasted polemic, decorated by maps of Middle East countries, bursts of free verse and a swirl of music that, though well drummed by Kareem Samara, is too loud. That makes it hard to hear Mahfouz and her co-performer Laura Hanna — a relief.
Stef O’Driscoll’s inventive production will appeal to a young audience.

cn.t: Mahfouz's lecture-gig hybrid earns modest praise for its ambitious blend of poetry, music, and anti-colonial politics, though critics find the whirlwind format overstuffed and more educational than engaging.
